title: Deflection & Attraction
concept: Drag a defender away, or lure the king onto a bad square.

glossary.definition: Forcing a defending piece away from its post, usually with a check or a capture it has to answer.

summary: Ask which enemy piece is holding everything together. A check or capture that forces it to move is a deflection; a sacrifice that drags the king onto a bad square is an attraction.

narration: Black's queen grabs the pawn on b4, right in front of your queen. She looks safe: the rook on b8 guards her.
Rook to c8, check! A sacrifice, and the piece that takes it is the rook that guards the queen.
The rook takes on c8 and leaves the b-file. The queen has lost her guard.
Queen takes queen. You dragged the defender away: that's a deflection.

guided.hint: Your rook on g1 can take on g8 with check. Where does the king end up, and which square can your other rook reach?
guided.explanation: Rook takes g8, check! When the king takes back it lands on g8, exactly where your other rook can strike: rook to e8 is checkmate, and your king on h6 covers g7 and h7. You lured the king onto the back row.

guided.hint: Black's rook on d8 is guarded only by the queen on d5. Can you give a check that makes the queen move?
guided.explanation: Queen to e7 is check, and Black's best block is the queen on f7. But she was the rook's only guard: once she leaves the d-file, your queen takes the rook on d8.

guided.hint: White's king on h1 is short of space. What if you could drag it onto h2, right on your queen's diagonal?
guided.explanation: Rook takes h2, check! The king has to take, and that pulls it onto h2. Now queen to h4 is checkmate: your bishop on e3 covers g1, and the queen covers the rest. You lured the king into the open.
